Grown-up guide · 1 of 2

Pictures make the plan easy to see

Little ones live in the now. A short row of pictures shows them what is happening, what comes next and when it's done. They can point to it, carry it and move it themselves. Bigger kids can run their own mornings with a checklist they helped write. Use as few or as many cards as your family needs.

239

picture cards

181 for ages 0–5 (feelings, plan words and the screens pair work at any age) and 58 big-kid cards for ages 5–12.

6

chart layouts

Vertical strips, horizontal strips, a first–then board, morning and bedtime charts and a Today board.

4

colorways

Rainbow, Soft and Navy in the Color file; Simple, a white ink-saver, in the Low-ink file.

2

paper sizes

US Letter and A4. Cards stay 2.2 in (5.6 cm) on both, so every card fits every chart.

+

make it yours

Blank, word-free and photo-frame cards, second copies of busy cards, and blank charts you can type into.

16

routine groups

Morning to bedtime, feelings, plan words, out and about, and four big-kid groups. Monday and Sunday starts.

Set up in 2 minutes

1. Pick one routine you already do, like bedtime.
2. Print its cards and one chart at 100% (Actual size).
3. Lay three cards on the chart and start tonight. Laminating and dots can wait for the weekend.

What your child is practicing

Knowing what comes next. Taking a real job in their own day by moving a card to All done. Words for everyday things and feelings. There are no tests and nothing to get right.

Play first
Screens later

Play first, screens later

Screens get their own steady spot in the day, after play. The spot doesn't grow or shrink with jobs or behavior, so it never becomes the prize. What we do next and 5 more minutes cards help with the switch. The tablet is a plain, generic picture: no brands, no apps. For reference, the World Health Organization (2019) suggests no screen time for babies under 1 and no more than 1 hour a day for ages 2–4.

Grown-up guide · 2 of 2

The cards are the start of a conversation

A routine card is something to talk about together, not a replacement for talking. A card is an invitation, never a test. Start with the first three ideas; add the others when you like. There's nothing to get right.

Shoes on

Say what you see

"Shoes on! Blue shoes." Name the card as your child touches it.

Brush teeth

Pause and wait

"First teeth, then…" and wait a few seconds. A point, a look or a sound is an answer.

Bath time

Repeat and add one word

Your child says "bath." You say "warm bath." One word more than they said.

Puzzle

Offer a choice

Hold up two play cards: "Blocks or puzzle?" Let them pick and put it on the chart.

Feed the pet

Follow their lead

If they grab the dog card, talk about the dog. The plan can wait ten seconds.

Sing a song

Sing and gesture

Make up a tidy-up tune or a wave for "all done." Same song, same moment, every day.

Every language counts

Talk, sign, sing and read in the language you know best. Every language counts. Family words, home languages and pet names all belong on these cards. A sign, a point, a tap on a card, even a "no": it all counts as communicating. Saying the card's word the same way every time, or using the cards quietly side by side, counts too.

If interest fades

Put the cards away for a week, then bring back just two. Let your child choose which routine gets a chart, or hand them the job of moving the cards. Most children love 2–3 of these; that's normal.

Use them by age

Start small, grow the plan with your child

Every child is different, so use these as starting points, not targets. If a step feels like too much, drop back to fewer cards. If it feels too easy, hand over more of the plan.

0–12 months

One card, one moment

Show a single card right before it happens and say the word: "Bath!" Hold it where your baby can look, then do the thing together. The grown-up holds the card.

1–2 years

First, then

Two cards on the first–then board, laid on top (no dots under 3). "First shoes, then park." Let your toddler carry the "then" card to the door.

2–3 years

A strip of three or four

Pick one routine and use the vertical strip. Your child moves each card to All done or into the pocket. Keep the same order every day.

3–5 years

Morning and bedtime charts

Up to nine steps. Let them choose the order of two steps, and add a feelings card: "How are you feeling this morning?"

5–8 years

Big-kid cards and checklists

Switch to the 5–12 cards or the weekly checklist. They tick, you notice. Swap in a card when something new is happening.

8–12 years

They write the plan

Blank cards and the fillable checklist let them set their own routine. Agree together where screens fit in the day, and keep that spot steady.

Change of plan

Change of plan

Slip this card in when the day changes. It shows something new is coming, before it arrives.

Wait

Wait

For the in-between moments: the kettle, the line at the store, a sibling's turn.

Calm

Feelings check-in

Offer two or three feelings cards and let your child point. Then pick a calm-down card together.

Every child grows on their own timeline. If you have questions about your child's development, talk with your pediatrician.

Print guide

What to print (and what to skip)

You don't need to print everything. Pick one colorway, print the cards for the routines you use, and add one chart.

Printer settings

Print at 100% / Actual size, never "Fit to page", so cards stay 2.2 in (5.6 cm). White cardstock, 65–110 lb (176–300 gsm). Landscape pages turn by themselves in most printers; if not, choose "Auto-rotate".

Your two files

This is the Low-ink file. The Color file has the same cards and charts in Rainbow, Soft and Navy. Both come in US Letter and A4.

What you can type

Open this PDF in free Adobe Acrobat Reader (computer or phone). You can type labels on blank, word-free and photo cards, chart titles and names, and big-kid jobs, and tick the checklist boxes. Accents work (á, ñ, ü); for other alphabets, write by hand. Colors and pictures can't be changed. Bonus Canva-ready PNGs are on the free bonus page.

2

Start tonight: print just 2 pages

Page 15 (bedtime cards) and page 52 (the vertical strip). Pick four cards from that page, like Bath time, Pajamas, Brush teeth and Lullaby, lay them on the strip, and move each one to All done as you go. Everything else can wait.

Laminate, stick and store

Make them last for years

1

Print on cardstock

White cardstock, 65–110 lb (176–300 gsm), at 100%. Let ink dry a few minutes.

2

Laminate the sheet

3–5 mil pouches. Laminate the full page, then cut. No laminator? Wide clear packing tape or a page protector works.

3

Cut with a sealed edge

Leave about 1/8 in (3 mm) of sealed plastic and round the corners so they're soft in little hands.

4

Dots, ages 3+

Rough (hook) dots on chart slots, soft (loop) dots on card backs. 3/4 in (19 mm) coin dots fit best.

5

Under 3: no dots

Lay cards on top of the chart, drop finished cards in the All done pocket, or slide the chart into a page protector and tuck cards in.

6

Store and reuse

Storage labels go on pouches or envelopes. Laminated blanks and checklists take dry-erase markers.

Safety for little hands

  • A grown-up stays close and keeps the pieces. Routine cards are a together activity, not a toy to leave in the crib or bed.
  • Every card is 2.2 in (5.6 cm) square, bigger than a toilet-paper tube opening, a common rule of thumb for small parts with children under 3. Don't shrink the cards when printing, and don't cut them into smaller pieces.
  • Hook-and-loop dots, laminating scraps and loose plastic are small parts. Check dots before each play; remove any that lift. Keep spares out of reach, and skip magnets for any child who still puts things in their mouth.
  • Hang charts low enough to reach without climbing, and away from blind cords. Every card follows our published safety rules.
toilet-paper
tube opening
about 1.25 in

Size check

Measure the dashed square with a ruler after printing. If it's 2.2 in (5.6 cm) on each side, you printed at the right size and every card is bigger than a toilet-paper tube opening. If it's smaller, reprint at 100% / Actual size.

All agesPhoto-frame cards: print, glue, laminateSimple

Photo cards

For the things only your family has: your front door, the car seat, grandma's house, the family pet.

1. Snap a photo of the real thing, close up and in good light.
2. Print it about 1.6 × 1.4 in (4 × 3.5 cm): a wallet-size photo print trimmed down works, or print the photo on plain paper at that size.
3. Glue it inside the dashed frame with a glue stick and let it dry flat.
4. Label by hand, or type in Acrobat Reader before printing this page. Then laminate and cut.

Cut on the gray lines · Grown-up keeps the pieces · Cards are 2.2 in / 5.6 cm, big-piece size for under-3s · Glue photos before laminating playbeforepixels.com

Extras

Today markers and an All done pocket

Today
Today
Today markers. Cut out and laminate. Ages 3+: stick a hook-and-loop dot on the back and move it along the day chips on the Today board. Under 3: lay it on the chip.

All done pocket. Cut on the dashed line. Fold the three glue flaps back along the gray lines and glue them to the chart or the wall, leaving the top open. Finished cards drop inside. No dots needed, so it suits under-3s.
GLUE FLAP
All done!
